source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF homepage/code link and the repository README both identify the paper/replication project. gh read-only metadata and the recursive tree were checked after the inventory row (no_public_source_found) and absent local source directory. Exact or near-exact public visual material exists for Figure 1, Figure 2 styling/model output, Figure 9, Figure 10, and Figure 11; the same notebook grammar supports Figures 7–8. The repository has no paper TeX, Table 1–3 generator, Figure 5/6 final renderer, or Figure 7/8 composite wrapper. The copy experiment files are relevant to Figure 4’s data but the inspected generic plot helper visibly differs from the paper figure, so it is not marked exact.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Charts use local semantic palettes: Blues/Reds lightness for PG19/random and m, blue/orange/green for support geometry, fixed model-family colors for the cell-volume tail, and tab10 order colors for n-fold distributions. Figure 1 token cells and Figure 6 proof regions use separate categorical red/blue systems. Tables remain black-and-white.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Most charts and tables are vector PDF paths/text. Figure 1 is a raster plane XObject embedded in a vector page, and Figure 6 is a small raster diagram XObject; captions and surrounding mathematics remain vector.
paper_style.style_consistency: Within each figure family the grammar is consistent, especially Figure 2→7→8 and Figure 3→10→11. Across families, color semantics are local rather than global: blue can mean PG19, Ball, Pythia, or a token cell. Main tables share model column ordering and booktabs rules, while chart typography is sans-serif and table/caption typography is serif.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Plane cut of the embedding space E of Qwen-2 (0.5B) (Yang et al., 2024), passing through the final token embeddings of “The quick brown fox”, “https://”, and “In a distant future” (red markers). Colors encode, for each pixel, the most probable next token via the model’s output projection (decoder readout). This induces regions E_t annotated by < t >. Only tokens whose regions have the largest areas are annotated for readability. The three embeddings fall respectively in E_jumps, E_www, and E_,, i.e. the predicted next tokens are <jumps>, <www>, and <,>.

color.semantic_mapping: Each region color identifies an argmax next-token cell; red/white markers identify the three prompt embeddings.

encodings.text: direct token labels and three prompt text boxes

figures.data_and_statistics: A qualitative PCA plane through the three final-token embeddings. The raster plane evaluates the decoder readout at a 200×200 grid (the public script default), assigns each pixel its most probable next token, and overlays three concrete prompt embeddings. No aggregate estimate, denominator, uncertainty, or repeated run is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 4, §3.1 “Partitioning the Embedding Space by the most Likely Next Token” defines E_t and immediately uses Figure 1 as its plane-cut illustration; §3.2 then lifts the one-token cells to prompt regions E_t^m, which feed Theorem 4.6 and Corollary 4.7.
design_strengths: One view connects support geometry, decoder cells, and concrete prompt embeddings.
Direct token labels avoid a second token legend and make the intended argmax semantics visible.
The red marker and white outline are redundant with the prompt text boxes.
design_weaknesses: A two-dimensional PCA slice cannot stand in for high-dimensional cell volume or sequence accessibility.
Region boundaries depend on finite grid resolution, plane bounds, and the visible top-token selection.
PCA variance explained, sampling uncertainty, and the relationship between displayed area and high-dimensional volume are absent.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use “colored argmax regions + direct token labels + concrete prompt markers” to give an abstract decoder partition a readable geometric interface, while stating explicitly that the view is a slice rather than a volume estimate.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Mean accessibility for a) PG19 and b) random target sequences of length n as a function of the number of trainable memory vectors m. For each m, we fit a sigmoid (solid) and mark n50 where the fit crosses 0.5 (vertical dashed line). (c) n50(m) for PG19 (blue) and random (red), with linear fits (dashed).

color.semantic_mapping: Blue sequential shades encode PG19 memory lengths m=1…5; red sequential shades encode random memory lengths m=1…5; blue/red and black/gray in panel c distinguish domains and their fits.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: a/b upper right for m; c upper left for fit key

encodings.x: target length n in a/b; memory length m in c
encodings.y: mean accessibility in a/b; n at accessibility 50% in c
encodings.color: PG19 versus random and five m values
encodings.shape: raw observations, PG19 circle, random x
encodings.line: sigmoid fits, raw dotted traces, vertical n50 and c linear fits
encodings.facet: a PG19, b random, c derived n50(m)
encodings.text: panel letters, m legend, and fit labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Qwen2.5-1.5B accessibility experiment. For every (n,m), the paper averages exact greedy-generation success over 20 target strings, with PG19 contiguous spans and vocabulary-uniform random strings as the two target sources; m is 1…5. Solid curves are sigmoid fits, vertical dashed lines mark the 0.5 crossing n50, and c linearly fits the five n50 values per domain. The page reports PG19 slope a=79.56 with R²=0.999 and random slope a=36.38 with R²=0.995; no error bars, seeds, or target-level spread are shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 7, §5.1 defines the frozen-weight/optimized-memory cramming test and its 20-target mean; Figure 2a/b tests the fixed-m threshold, while Figure 2c tests the predicted linear n50(m) relation. Table 1 first-row ratios and Appendix Figures 7–8 extend the same chain.
design_strengths: The left curves preserve threshold shape while the right panel exposes the theory-relevant derived quantity.
PG19/random use stable vertical placement and color semantics, making the domain comparison immediate.
Raw dots remain visible beneath the fitted sigmoid instead of hiding fit misspecification.
design_weaknesses: Five memory values rely mainly on color lightness, which is fragile in grayscale and for color-vision deficiency.
The raw points have no uncertainty definition or sample-count annotation in the figure.
The fitted crossing is summarized without a confidence range or a direct threshold table.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair condition-specific transition curves with a compact derived-threshold panel: keep raw observations, mark the crossing used by the theory, then fit the crossing quantity separately.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Conceptual example of using the cell-volume distribution to tighten the upper bound. Rather than assuming equal-volume cells (Dirac mass), we take the n-fold convolution of the empirical one-step volume distribution D1 (light violet) and track when the median of Dn (violet dashed) drops below the threshold (black dashed).

color.semantic_mapping: Light-to-dark violet encodes D1 through D4; black dashed reference marks the threshold.

encodings.x: one-step/sequence cell-volume proportion |E_t|/|E| on a log scale
encodings.line: step profiles and dashed threshold/median references

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual profile, not a model-specific sample distribution. It illustrates the empirical one-step cell-volume distribution D1 and its multiplicative n-fold convolutions Dn, with a median crossing a precision-dependent accessibility threshold. No observations, sample denominator, uncertainty, or actual architecture is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 8, §5.3 introduces the equal-volume approximation and the median criterion; Figure 3 is the mechanism bridge to Appendix H’s 50M-sample cell-volume estimates, Table 3, and Figures 10–11, and explains the Non-uniform Cells row of Table 1.
design_strengths: Log x scale makes the many-orders-of-magnitude volume contraction visible.
The Dn color progression and threshold/median dashed semantics map directly to the written criterion.
A low-load conceptual panel separates mechanism explanation from the dense empirical tail plots.
design_weaknesses: The curves are explicitly conceptual, so their height and positions must not be treated as an empirical model result.
The threshold value and exact roles of the visible vertical references are not numerically labeled.
The density label does not provide enough information to reconstruct normalization from the panel alone.
figures.reusable_pattern: Explain a distributional refinement as “base distribution → n-fold convolution → threshold crossing” before showing the full empirical distribution, using a log axis for multiplicative scales.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Models are trained to copy strings up to a maximum length (grey dashed) and evaluated on generating the exact copy of longer strings. We report exact-match copying accuracy versus string length. For each model, we fit a sigmoid to the accuracy curve (continuous lines) and report the corresponding R2 .

color.semantic_mapping: Seven model curves use distinct colors; gray dashed line denotes the training maximum-length reference.

encodings.color: model identity; gray for training maximum
encodings.line: solid sigmoid model curves; gray dashed training-length reference
encodings.text: model names and fit R² in legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Synthetic exact-copying length generalization. Training strings have length at most 50; training stops at 100% exact-match on length 50 or after 10K optimization steps, then seven pretrained model families are evaluated on longer unseen strings in-context. Each solid curve is a sigmoid fit and its legend R² is fit quality; the plot contains no error band, seed spread, or independent replication.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 9, §5.4 moves from Corollary 4.7/cramming to Corollary 4.11/copying; Figure 4 supplies the failure evidence for the claim that every fixed transformer exhibits an accessibility limitation, followed by the conclusion on p.9.
design_strengths: A common length/accuracy frame makes model-specific transition locations visually comparable.
The training cutoff reference separates in-distribution training lengths from extrapolation.
The abrupt decline is visually legible without requiring a new panel or metric.
design_weaknesses: Transition lengths are not labeled or tabulated, so exact threshold comparison requires digitization.
R² describes sigmoid fit quality rather than uncertainty in copying accuracy and varies substantially by model.
The gray reference has no number label in the panel; the exact training maximum comes from adjacent prose.
figures.reusable_pattern: Overlay model-specific extrapolation failure curves on one shared length axis and mark the training support with a reference line; pair the visual with an explicit threshold/replication summary.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5. Maximal radius R of the internal representations of the transformer for various input lengths.

color.semantic_mapping: The same blue line encodes maximal radius R in every model panel; model identity is carried by panel titles.

encodings.facet: seven model panels in a 3+3+1 layout

figures.data_and_statistics: For each of seven models, the plot tracks the maximal radius R of internal representations as the maximum sampled input length grows. The visible curves rise rapidly at short lengths and then plateau. It is a maximum statistic, with no quantiles, uncertainty, repeated-run spread, or sample count shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A p.14–15 formalizes transformer layers and the bounded embedding-support setting; Figure 5 checks radius stability, which is then instantiated as r in Table 2 and used by the geometry bounds in Figure 9/Table 1.
design_strengths: Small multiples expose whether the bounded-radius assumption stabilizes across model families.
A long x range to roughly 4000 makes the plateau visible rather than stopping at the first rise.
Uniform line grammar keeps the diagnostic focused on convergence.
design_weaknesses: Panel-specific y ranges prevent direct visual comparison of absolute R across models.
A maximum alone is sensitive to outliers and gives no sampling uncertainty.
The caption omits model list, sampling count, and the operational definition of internal representation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a common sampling-budget x axis in model small multiples to diagnose convergence of a support statistic, then publish the selected constant separately with its sampling protocol.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6. Decomposition of the cone in Eδ and Fδ.

color.semantic_mapping: Red cap Eδ, blue cone/Fδ, and black/gray axis, chord, and angle annotations identify the proof pieces.

encodings.line: cone boundary, cap arc, chord, axis, and δ angle arc
encodings.text: Eδ, Fδ, x1, and δ direct labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual two-dimensional diagram with no data or scale. It partitions the d-dimensional cone proof into the conical portion Eδ and spherical-cap portion Fδ, which are integrated separately.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 22, Appendix F.2 Steps 3–4 use the Eδ and Fδ split before Step 5 sums the volume contributions; the result feeds Proposition F.3/Corollary F.5 and the Cone enclosure row in Table 1.
design_strengths: Color regions correspond one-to-one with the two subsequent proof integrals.
The chord, axis, and δ arc expose the geometric boundaries used by the formulas.
Direct labels make the diagram interpretable without a legend.
design_weaknesses: A 2-D sketch is not to scale for a d-dimensional cone or its volumes.
The short caption does not define δ, radius, or the spherical-cap condition.
The figure object is a small raster XObject, so zoomed labels have lower fidelity than surrounding vector mathematics.
figures.reusable_pattern: Color and label each proof subregion with the same symbols used in the derivation, so later integrals can be traced back to a visible geometric object.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. Mean accessibility for a) PG19 and b) random target sequences of length n as a function of the number of trainable memory vectors m. For each m, we fit a sigmoid (solid) and mark n50 where the fit crosses 0.5 (vertical dashed line). (c) n50(m) for PG19 (blue) and random (red), with linear fits (dashed). Results shown for the Pythia model suite at different scales A) 160M, B) 410M, C) 1B.

color.semantic_mapping: Within each model block, blue shades encode PG19 m values and red shades encode random m values; black/gray fits and panel titles complete the key.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: a/b upper right and c upper left per model block

encodings.x: n in a/b; m in c
encodings.y: accessibility in a/b; n at 50% accessibility in c
encodings.shape: raw dots, PG19 circle, random x
encodings.line: sigmoid, vertical n50, and c linear fits
encodings.facet: three model blocks A/B/C, each with a/b/c
encodings.text: model block labels and repeated legends

figures.data_and_statistics: The Figure 2 experiment is repeated for Pythia-160M, Pythia-410M, and Pythia-1B. Each block uses PG19/random targets, five trainable memory lengths, mean accessibility over the target set, sigmoid crossings, and linear n50 fits. Block-specific x/y ranges change with scale; no error bars or run-level variation are shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 7 Figure 2 is the Qwen2.5-1.5B canonical example; Appendix G.3 p.24 and Figure 7 extend the same evidence to Pythia scales. Table 1/2 provide the matching model geometry, while this figure tests cross-size robustness rather than component deletion.
design_strengths: Reusing Figure 2’s a/b/c grammar lowers the cost of cross-size comparison.
Each model block retains both raw accessibility curves and the derived n50 slope.
The block title makes model identity independent of the color channel.
design_weaknesses: Nine panels and repeated legends make text small and visually dense.
Different block ranges impede direct absolute-height comparison.
Thirty visible threshold references and many raw points still do not expose threshold uncertainty.
figures.reusable_pattern: Freeze a canonical transition-plot grammar, then replicate it as model blocks so robustness changes the facet, not the reader’s interpretation rules.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8. Mean accessibility for a) PG19 and b) random target sequences of length n as a function of the number of trainable memory vectors m. For each m, we fit a sigmoid (solid) and mark n50 where the fit crosses 0.5 (vertical dashed line). (c) n50(m) for PG19 (blue) and random (red), with linear fits (dashed). Results shown for three architectures A) Qwen-2.5, B) Gemma-3, C) Llama-3.2.

color.semantic_mapping: Within each architecture block, blue shades encode PG19 m values and red shades encode random m values; architecture is a direct block title, not a color.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: a/b upper right and c upper left per architecture block

encodings.x: n in a/b; m in c
encodings.y: accessibility in a/b; n at 50% accessibility in c
encodings.shape: raw dots, PG19 circle, random x
encodings.line: sigmoid, vertical n50, and c linear fits
encodings.facet: three architecture blocks A/B/C, each with a/b/c
encodings.text: architecture block labels and repeated legends

figures.data_and_statistics: The Figure 2 experiment is repeated for Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, and Llama-3.2. Each architecture block uses the same PG19/random target sources, five m values, target-level mean accessibility, sigmoid crossing, and c-panel linear fit. No error bars, seeds, or architecture-interaction uncertainty are displayed.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 7 Figure 2 establishes the canonical Qwen accessibility result; Appendix G.3 Figure 8 checks the same pattern across three architectures. The model constants in Table 2 and geometry bounds in Figure 9 provide adjacent architectural context, but Figure 8 itself encodes accessibility only.
design_strengths: Stable panel semantics make architecture generalization easy to scan.
Architecture is encoded redundantly by block title and position, leaving blue/red for target source and m.
Derived n50 fits remain visible beside the raw curves.
design_weaknesses: The full-page composite repeats axis labels and legends nine times.
Architecture blocks do not share identical ranges, making absolute comparisons costly.
The fitted crossing lacks residuals, uncertainty, or an explicit interaction test.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use block-level architecture facets with a frozen accessibility grammar, preserving the meaning of colors for target source and memory length across architectures.

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9. Upper bound on C for different support geometry —Ball (blue), Cone (green), Ellipsoid (orange)—, estimated using 10K randomly sampled input strings of maximum length ℓ. Sampling prompts longer than ℓ ≈ 500 suffices to estimate the upper bound. Pythia models for different sizes: a) 160M b) 410M, c) 1B and support for different model architectures d–e) Qwen (0.5B, 1.5B) f) Llama 1B, g) Gemma 270M.

color.semantic_mapping: Ball blue, Ellipsoid orange, and Cone green identify support geometry; line style redundantly distinguishes the same three cases.

encodings.x: maximum sampled input length ℓ in tokens
encodings.line: Ball solid, Ellipsoid dotted, Cone dashed
encodings.facet: seven model panels a–g in a 3×3 grid
encodings.text: panel letters and model titles; shared geometry legend

figures.data_and_statistics: For each model and support geometry, C is estimated from 10K randomly sampled input strings at increasing maximum length ℓ. Ball, Cone, and Ellipsoid are the three enclosure calculations; the plot examines convergence as ℓ grows. The rendered panel titles show f) Gemma-3-270M and g) Llama-3.2-1B, while the PDF caption lists f) Llama 1B and g) Gemma 270M; the visual audit follows the panel titles and records the caption mismatch. The caption says ℓ≈500 is sufficient, while main-text §5.2 says ℓ≈1000 is sufficient in practice; neither is an uncertainty estimate.
figures.evidence_relation: Page 8 §5.2 introduces support sampling and points to Figure 9; Appendix G.4 supplies the geometry/precision details. Figure 9 validates the constants used in Table 2 and the support-refined rows of Table 1, not empirical copying accuracy.
design_strengths: Geometry is encoded by both color and solid/dotted/dashed line, preserving black-and-white distinction.
The shared legend leaves panel space for trajectories and the model titles identify every facet.
Long-length plateaus make sampling stabilization visible.
design_weaknesses: Panel-specific y ranges make cross-model absolute height comparisons easy to misread.
No Monte Carlo error bars or replicate-sampling spread are shown.
The two blank grid cells and the 500-versus-1000 wording discrepancy leave avoidable interpretation cost.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use geometry-specific line styles plus a shared legend in small multiples to audit convergence of a theoretical bound under increasing sampling budget.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10. Relative volumes of decoder cells across tokens (log-log). For each model, tokens are sorted by estimated cell volume (largest on the left). A small set of tokens (typically < 10^2) accounts for a large fraction of the support volume, while most tokens (10^4–10^5) have tiny individual volumes (often 10^−6–10^−8 of the support).

color.semantic_mapping: Each model receives a fixed color; adjacent hues group Pythia, Qwen, Llama, and Gemma families.

encodings.x: token rank sorted by decreasing cell-volume proportion
encodings.y: proportion of samples in the token cell

figures.data_and_statistics: Appendix H estimates each token’s decoder-cell proportion from sampled points in the ellipsoid support. The source plot retains the first 100 ranks and log-spaced tail ranks for each model, then overlays the seven ranked profiles on log-log axes. The displayed tail is therefore a visualization subsample, not a count of all plotted tokens; no sampling error is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 5.3 motivates non-uniform cells; Appendix H computes the one-step proportions; Figure 10 exposes the long tail that feeds Table 3 top-k examples, Figure 11 convolutions, and Table 1’s Non-uniform Cells refinement.
design_strengths: Log-log rank coordinates show both head concentration and many-decade tail behavior.
The source explicitly uses dense head ranks plus log-spaced tail ranks to reduce log-axis sampling artifacts.
A single shared coordinate frame makes family profiles directly overlaid.
design_weaknesses: Seven profiles rely only on color and legend, so overlap is difficult in grayscale.
Tail point subsampling changes visual point density and is not called out in the PDF caption.
The y-axis is a sample proportion proxy for cell volume, so its interpretation still depends on Appendix H.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a distribution spanning many orders of magnitude, sort by the quantity of interest, keep the head dense, sample the tail logarithmically, and state the subsampling rule next to the plot.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11. Distribution of n-sequences volumes proportions by estimating the n-fold convolution of the empirical one-step volume distribution D for different models: a) Pythia-160M, b) Pythia-410M, c) Pythia-1B, d) Qwen2.5 0.5B, e) Qwen2.5 1.5B, f) Llama3.2 1B, g) Gemma 270M.

color.semantic_mapping: The first six tab10 colors encode convolution order n=1…6; model identity is encoded by panel title.

encodings.x: volume proportion |E_t|/|E| on a log scale
encodings.y: Probability density in the PDF label
encodings.facet: seven model panels a–g in a 3×3 grid
encodings.text: shared n legend and model titles

figures.data_and_statistics: For each model, the empirical one-step volume distribution D is convolved multiplicatively to obtain n-fold distributions. The PDF shows n=1…6 normalized step profiles across seven models. The inspected source cell uses 70 log bins, a compression budget n=2000, and uniform weights; its histogram height is normalized bin mass while the PDF y label says Probability density, so density-versus-bin-mass semantics are not fully explicit. No error or approximation band is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix H one-step estimates and Table 3 feed Figure 11; its model/order distributions instantiate the mechanism introduced in Figure 3 and explain how non-uniform cells tighten the Table 1 upper bound.
design_strengths: Identical log-x semantics across seven panels make the convolution shift easy to compare.
A shared legend keeps the dense panels from repeating six labels.
Step curves preserve distribution shape better than a single median summary.
design_weaknesses: Six colors in small panels have limited grayscale and color-vision robustness.
The PDF’s “Probability density” label and source’s normalized histogram mass are not fully reconciled.
The PDF uses six orders while the inspected notebook default is max_k=4; the final parameter is not stated in the caption.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show successive distribution transforms as same-axis step overlays in model small multiples, and publish bin normalization, compression, and order range alongside the figure.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Ratio between the theoretical upper bound on the slope (using the infinity norm) and the empirical one for natural texts (PG19), across various models. Rows correspond to different enclosure strategies, and columns to the evaluated models. The detailed theoretical analysis is provided in Appendix F.

tables.uncertainty: None. All entries are point ratios; no empirical-slope error, sample count, repetition, or interval is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Theoretical upper-bound slope divided by empirical PG19 natural-text slope, across Ball, Cone, Ellipsoid, Ellipsoid + Non-uniform Cells, and Ellipsoid + variable ε. Model columns are Pythia 160M/410M/1B, Qwen-2.5 0.5B/1.5B, Llama-3.2 1B, and Gemma-3 270M. Values are point estimates with mixed one/two-decimal presentation; the fourth row is bold.
tables.evidence_relation: Pages 8–9, §§5.2–5.3 move from Corollary 4.7’s ball/equal-cell approximation to support and cell-volume refinements; Table 1 quantifies those rows, with Appendix F deriving geometry and Appendices G/H supplying constants and distributions.
design_strengths: Stable family/size columns align with Table 2.
Rows expose successive enclosure/refinement assumptions on one control axis.
Bold fourth row makes the non-uniform-cell tightening immediately visible in black and white.
design_weaknesses: Mixed precision such as 14.1, 14.01, and 14.3 implies more uniform decimal formatting than the table provides.
Ratios omit the underlying empirical slopes and their variability.
Several entries exceed the abstract’s unqualified “factor less than 10” wording, so row scope must be read carefully.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep model columns fixed across the main ratio table and its appendix constants table; put geometric approximations in rows and bold the refinement that changes the bound.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2. Model constants used to estimate slope upper-bound ratios in Table 1. The dimensionality d and vocabulary size |V| are determined by the model architecture, while r and θ are estimated in Section 5.2.

tables.uncertainty: No errors or repetitions. d and |V| are architecture constants; r and θ are estimates from the support sampling procedure in Section 5.2.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix G.1 p.23 supplies the constants consumed by the Ball/Cone/Ellipsoid formulas in Appendix F and the ratio rows in Table 1; the architecture-versus-sampling split mirrors the setup in §5.2.
design_strengths: Exactly reuses Table 1’s model-family and size ordering.
Separates architecture-fixed quantities from geometry estimates in named rows.
Compact layout makes bound reconstruction possible without searching through prose.
design_weaknesses: The estimated r and θ have no Monte Carlo spread or sample-count column.
θ has no unit/definition cue in the header beyond the symbol.
The table does not carry the precision ε or sampling length used alongside these constants.
tables.reusable_pattern: Publish a narrow constants table with the same column order as the main result table and explicitly distinguish architecture facts from sampled geometric estimates.

tables.evidence_relation: Appendix H p.25 describes the decoder-cell volume estimator; Table 3 p.26 gives top-k token examples, which are expanded by the full ranked profiles in Figure 10 and by the convolution distributions in Figure 11.
design_strengths: Token identity and normalized cell proportion are kept in one compact row per model.
Explicit whitespace/control/Unicode notation makes otherwise invisible tokens auditable.
The top-k table complements the long-tail chart with concrete semantic examples.
design_weaknesses: Long token lists wrap across a wide second column and are costly to scan laterally.
Top five values cannot describe the tail or establish a full token ranking.
No Monte Carlo error or denominator is displayed in the table itself.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair a top-k token/value table with an all-token ranked plot, and define a stable escaping convention for whitespace, control, and Unicode tokens.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The visual sequence is geometry intuition (Figure 1), fixed-memory threshold evidence (Figure 2), bound refinement (Table 1 and Figure 3), and copying failure (Figure 4), followed by appendix validation of radius, proof geometry, constants, cross-model accessibility, support sampling, and cell-volume tails/convolutions (Figures 5–11 and Tables 2–3).
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use an italicized numbered label followed by a descriptive sentence. Figures 1–3 and 7–11 mostly define setup and encoding; Figure 10 is the clearest caption-level main finding. Most captions omit uncertainty and seed details; Figure 4 reports R2 fit quality, not an uncertainty interval.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Table 1 and Table 2 share a two-level model-family/size header and the same seven-column order. Table 3 uses a single Model plus long token-list column. Booktabs top/header/bottom rules and no cell color form the common table grammar.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 1 and the theorem sections define decoder cells and prompt regions; Figure 2 tests the memory-length prediction; Table 1 refines its slope bound; Figure 4 tests the copying consequence. There is no component-removal ablation; appendix sensitivity is expressed through geometry, sampling length, model scale, and cell-volume order.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main Figure 2 is a Qwen2.5-1.5B instance; Figures 7–8 reproduce its accessibility grammar across sizes and architectures. Table 1’s compact ratios require Table 2 constants and Figures 9–11/Appendix H sampling details; Figure 3’s conceptual mechanism is empirically expanded by Table 3 and Figures 10–11.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: PDF body/captions/tables consistently use Nimbus Roman and Computer Modern math. Chart labels consistently use embedded sans-serif families (Myriad Pro, Segoe UI Variable, DejaVu Sans) with small sizes. Figure 1/6 raster assets introduce local font uncertainty but do not alter the page-level serif system.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Color is consistent within families, not across the paper. Blues/Reds identify dataset source and m in accessibility plots; blue/orange/green identify support geometry; model-family colors identify cell-volume profiles; tab10 identifies n. Direct labels and line styles partially compensate, but many identity mappings remain color dependent.

most_reusable_patterns: Figure 2/7/8: condition curves plus an explicit threshold and derived-summary panel.
Table 1/2: stable model-family/size columns reused across results and constants.
Figure 5/9/11: small multiples that put model or geometry in panels and reserve color/line style for the varying factor.
Figure 10: log-log ranked long-tail view with dense head and logarithmically sampled tail.
Figure 1/6: direct labels and colored proof/partition regions tied to formula symbols.
highest_value_objects: Figure 2: the shortest visual test of the fixed-m linear-threshold claim.
Table 1: the joint geometry/refinement versus empirical-slope decision surface.
Figure 4: the most direct multi-model visualization of long-copy failure.
Figures 10–11: the empirical tail and convolution evidence behind non-uniform-cell tightening.
failure_patterns: Most plots lack run-level, target-level, or Monte Carlo uncertainty; fitted crossings and geometric estimates are presented as single trajectories.
Color carries model/order identity in dense plots without enough line-style or direct-label redundancy for grayscale.
Table 1 mixes decimal precision and Table 3 wraps long token strings, increasing numeric and token-level audit cost.
Figure 3/5/6 omit key numeric or symbol definitions; Figure 9 has a 500-versus-1000 sampling-language mismatch; Figure 11 does not fully resolve density versus normalized bin-mass semantics.
The public copy runner is relevant to Figure 4’s experiment but its generic plotting helper differs from the PDF, illustrating the risk of treating an adjacent candidate as exact visual source.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper moves from embedding-plane and accessibility-threshold intuition to slope-ratio and copying-failure decisions, then uses appendix geometry and cell-volume small multiples to tighten and generalize the bound while leaving much of the uncertainty and final composite assembly outside the plotted objects.
